title: Prisons under pressure: purpose, drugs, staff and reform
label: 20 October 2026 · Oral evidence to the Justice Committee
summary: Charlie Taylor, HM Chief Inspector of Prisons, reviewed the state of the prison estate at the end of his tenure. He praised improvements in leadership and some prisons' programmes, but warned that purposeful activity has weakened, drugs (especially drone deliveries) and violence are rising, mental-health treatment and post-release support are patchy, and recruitment and procurement block basic repairs and staffing. He urged action on staffing, leadership, drug supply and rehabilitation to reduce reoffending and ease capacity pressures.

chapters.title: Overall state of the estate
chapters.takeaway: Leadership and some reforms have improved parts of the estate, but pressures from population, drugs and reduced activity make the system fragile.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Mr Taylor, after six years as chief inspector, is the Prison Service better or worse than when you started?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: It's mixed. During covid the service cooperated well with inspections, and leadership has improved in many places, but population pressures, rising drug use and too much time locked up make the system fragile.

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Security has improved—very few escapes—but issues such as drone deliveries of drugs and low purposeful activity threaten safety, rehabilitation and public protection.

turns.speaker: Warinder Juss
turns.text: You noted purposeful activity and drugs are big problems. Has purposeful activity improved since you last gave evidence?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Some prisons have improved, but nationally it's worse: budget cuts led to reduced education staff and fewer English and maths places, so provision is more fragile than before.

chapters.title: Purposeful activity and rehabilitation
chapters.takeaway: Reduced education and enrichment, plus too much time locked in cells, make rehabilitation weaker and may increase reoffending.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You argued time productively spent helps mental health and reduces reoffending—have things improved?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: No. Cuts since last October mean fewer teachers and courses, less English and maths, and more prisoners locked up with little to do—bad for mental health and for post-release employment chances.

turns.speaker: Warinder Juss
turns.text: Statistics show 34% of men and 50% of women locked up 22+ hours a day—what impact does that have?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Long-run harm: worsened mental health, boredom, drug use to pass time, and prisoners leaving unprepared to work—so they often reoffend quickly.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are there examples of good practice we can copy?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Yes: HMP Oakwood delegates responsibility to prisoners who earn it; Hatfield focuses on getting prisoners into real work; Haverigg builds local employer links; Chelmsford reduced drugs by improving basics.

turns.speaker: Mrs Russell
turns.text: Do prisons strike the right balance between estate-cutting work and work that leads to employment?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Not always. Some workshops are low-skill and offer no progression; successful places give realistic working days, link to employers and create continuity into release.

turns.speaker: Vikki Slade
turns.text: Children and young adults have a statutory minimum of 15 hours' education; many do less—why?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Long lock-up times, complex keep-apart lists and poor behaviour management reduce access to education; Parc is the exception with clear ethos, leadership and much higher attendance.

chapters.title: Drugs, drones and violence
chapters.takeaway: Drone deliveries and mobile phones are driving a drugs market inside prisons that increases debt, debt-related violence and instability.

turns.speaker: Tessa Munt
turns.text: Your report said prisons are unstable and unsafe without tackling demand—are current measures effective?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Both supply and demand must be tackled. Supply requires better co-ordination—Home Office, MoJ, police, NCA, MOD—and faster technological and physical responses to drones and phones.

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Target-hardening, good searching, cell moves, body scans, visitor searches and vigilance against staff corruption all matter; no single magic bullet exists.

turns.speaker: Tessa Munt
turns.text: Should we separate organised criminal bosses inside prisons?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: It should be tried: big players run supply and outside networks from custody, so making their custodial lives harder would reduce harm.

turns.speaker: Tessa Munt
turns.text: How much does drug addiction treatment in prison help?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: There are good examples—HMP Bristol's incentivised substance-free wing—but treatment must link to community provision; otherwise prisoners relapse on release.

turns.speaker: Warinder Juss
turns.text: Chelmsford reduced testing positives to about 15%—how did it do that?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: By getting the basics right: assertive management of risky prisoners, good searching, moving prisoners, CCTV, and proper follow-up on corruption and visitors.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is drug-driven debt the main cause of rising violence?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Yes—drugs create debts and violent enforcement; tackling drugs reduces violence, but staff numbers, training and specialist units for vulnerable prisoners are also key.

chapters.title: Vulnerable prisoners: mental health, women, children
chapters.takeaway: Prisons are often inappropriate for people with severe mental illness and many women and children have needs better met outside custody.

turns.speaker: Vikki Slade
turns.text: Are prisons able to manage people with serious mental illnesses safely?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Confidence is low. Transfers to hospital under the Mental Health Act are too slow—average waits around 80 days with cases taking far longer—and prisons are not therapeutic environments for very unwell people.

turns.speaker: Vikki Slade
turns.text: What happens to prisoners who need hospital care?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: They endure complex referral processes, long waits and sometimes end up in segregation units where conditions are inappropriate and harmful.

turns.speaker: Mrs Russell
turns.text: Do women in prison face different problems?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Yes—higher levels of trauma, addiction, homelessness and exploitation. Many women serve short sentences that offer little benefit; some would be better supported outside custody.

turns.speaker: Vikki Slade
turns.text: Should the women's population be reduced?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Where the public can be protected in the community and risk managed, community solutions are preferable; but serious offenders still need custody—it's for courts and Ministers to decide policy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: About children who commit sexual offences—are there effective custodial interventions?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: We rarely see effective treatment for serious sexual offences among children in custody; overall, evidence on the long-term effectiveness of some programmes is mixed.

turns.speaker: Vikki Slade
turns.text: Why is HMP Parc succeeding with children where others fail?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Parc has stable staff, clear rules, strong leadership, incentives for good behaviour and purposeful activities; that combination reduces lock-up time and improves learning.

chapters.title: Staffing, recruitment, procurement and capacity
chapters.takeaway: Recruitment, retention and the centralised procurement system are major constraints; building more cells without staff won't solve the crisis.

turns.speaker: Janet Daby
turns.text: How is morale among prison staff and what affects recruitment?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: It varies: morale is high where establishments feel safe and well-run, and very low where staff are overworked and fearful. Recruitment problems are regional and systemic and central recruitment often supplies unsuitable candidates.

turns.speaker: Mrs Russell
turns.text: You said governors want local recruitment—what stops that?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Centralised pipelines aim to fill vacancies quickly but governors say they can't vet people properly; pilots to localise recruitment exist but have had mixed evaluations.

turns.speaker: Dr Shastri-Hurst
turns.text: If a governor dismissed someone, can that person re-enter the service elsewhere without a flag?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Yes—flags and checks don't always prevent re-employment elsewhere, which frustrates governors who feel they lack control over staff quality.

turns.speaker: Warinder Juss
turns.text: Why is procurement so slow and expensive—are examples true?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Yes. Governors report excessive hoops: small repairs can cost many times more through formal procurement; a prison governor can spend far less without central permission than a headteacher can locally.

turns.speaker: Mrs Russell
turns.text: The Government plans 14,000 new places by 2031—can they staff and open them?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Building is one thing; staffing them is another. Many areas already struggle to recruit, and local pay rates for nearby roles (eg immigration centres) may make prison recruitment harder.

turns.speaker: Vikki Slade
turns.text: If most prisoners reoffend, should we build fewer cells and spend more on rehabilitation?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Yes—small improvements in reoffending (1–2%) through better drug treatment, purposeful activity and employment would substantially reduce population pressure, so rehabilitation deserves more focus.

chapters.title: IPP reform and final priorities
chapters.takeaway: Ending IPP is welcome but must be handled carefully case-by-case with clinical support, tailored release packages and routes to reduce risk.

turns.speaker: Dr Shastri-Hurst
turns.text: The Government will end IPP this Parliament—what would you advise to protect the public and prisoners' rights?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Ending IPP is right; do it carefully. Assess individual risk, provide prison-based interventions and ensure strong community packages and MAPPA arrangements on release to protect the public.

turns.speaker: Vikki Slade
turns.text: Many IPP prisoners wait for courses with long backlogs—how should recalls and course access change?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Increase course availability, use open prisons to reintegrate long-term institutionalised men, and avoid leaving people stuck because a required course isn't available for months.

turns.speaker: Tessa Munt
turns.text: You've worked with Amber Rudd's review—do you think reforms on security and staffing can be delivered?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Recommendations can be strong, but implementation depends on Ministers and resourcing; the system's culture and processes must be ready to act on change.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: As you hand over, what should your successor prioritise?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Tackle drugs and drones, fix recruitment and retention, free governors to lead rather than being tied up in procurement and admin, and focus on meaningful purposeful activity to reduce reoffending.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If you could fix one thing, what would it be?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Ideally no drugs, because that would change so much; practically, give governors accountability and better staffing so they can lead improvement.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Where can this Committee add most value?

turns.speaker: Witness
turns.text: Scrutinise recruitment and training pathways, and examine procurement constraints that stop governors delivering basic maintenance and improvement.
